newsitem.title: THAILAND: Small Thai rate cut seen after Lunar New Year.
newsitem.headline: Small Thai rate cut seen after Lunar New Year.

text.p: Thai banks are expected to trim interest rates marginally after Lunar New Year, which falls next month, as liquidity rises on the back of steadily increasing foreign fund inflows, bankers and analysts said on Friday.

"Foreign funds have steadily flowed into Thailand since early this yer. So there is the possibility that local interest rates will fall further," Singha Nikornpun, director and senior treasurer at Deutsche Bank AG, told Reuters.
The higher liquidity has sharply driven down the overnight interbank rate to 9.0-10.0 percent from 14.0-15.0 percent in late December, money market dealers said.
Bankers and analysts expect any rate cut to take place after the Lunar New Year on February 7 when liquidity usually tightens after high spending activity in the period leading to the festive season.
"Most banks are relucatant to reduce their interest rates now because they need to maintain funds to meet customer demand during the (festival) period," Nikorn said.
But the central bank, which has in the past advocated high rates to fight inflation, has made it known to bankers that it wants to see a gradual reduction in local rates.
Thailand's rates are among the highest in the region with the minimum lending rate (MLR) ranging from 13.50-13.25 percent.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan has also called for substantially lower interest rates to stimulate the economy. He expects interest rates to fall 1.5-2.0 percentage points this year in line with a global downtrend in rates.

"We expect only a slight cut in interest rates in the near term. The rates will be cut by 50 basis points at the most after the Lunar New Year," said Pattera Dilokrungthirapop, head of research at Socgen-Crosby Securities.
Analysts said any sharp fall in rates could create renewed pressure on inflation, which has subsided somewhat, and boost Thailand's already wide current account deficit.
Thai inflation grew by 5.9 percent last year, marginally higher than the 5.8 percent growth posted in 1995. The central bank expects the rate to dip to 4.8 percent in 1997.

The central bank has forecast that the Thai current account deficit for 1996 will widen to 8.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from 8.1 percent in 1995. It has also projected the deficit to narrow to 7.9 percent of GDP this year.

"Still, the closely watched current account deficit and a possible revival of inflation will prevent domestic interest rates from any significant drop," the Thai Farmers Research Center said in a new report.
The centre said it expected interests to fall by 50 basis points in the first half of this year.
